clue.text: Look, one saint in church right by that sacred enclosure?

indicators.note: the look, one and saint pieces sit inside the abbreviation for church

parts.note: CE is the abbreviation for the Church of England
lo is an old word for look or behold
the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone is told to look at a saint's image beside a holy precinct within a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'by' just joins the wordplay to the definition; R follows the church piece.
explanation.definitionFit: A cloistered walk enclosed by monastery or cathedral buildings is a covered, consecrated courtyard space.

clue.text: Frustrated ladies without help on the shelf?

indicators.note: used in its old sense of outside, so the rearranged ladies wrap around the help
frustrated ladies are upset and disordered, so their letters are rearranged

parts.note: aid means help

explanation.surface: Women who received no assistance feel thwarted and left unmarried.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, not lacking: the help sits inside the shuffled ladies that 'Frustrated' signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Something put aside has been shelved, left unused for later, the same idiom as being shelved.

clue.text: Dwelling in which soldier gets put up — given small room

indicators.note: in a down clue putting something up reads it from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: a GI is an American soldier
loo is British slang for a toilet, a small room

explanation.surface: A soldier is billeted in a house and allotted a tiny room.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put up' reverses GI to IG in this down clue; 'in which', 'gets' and 'given' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: An Inuit snow house is a domed dwelling built from blocks of packed snow.

clue.text: Fine sticky stuff a man needed for unnamed item

parts.note: fine thread is thin
gum is a sticky substance
Bob is a man's name

explanation.surface: A recipe calls for delicate glue and a man to fix some unnamed thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needed for' simply links the wordplay to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A whatsit or whatchamacallit is a jokey word for an object whose name escapes the speaker.

clue.text: Pearl's upset having minimal energy — setback in health terms

indicators.note: the letters of the name are knocked over and rearranged

parts.note: the possessive s counts as a letter here, giving six letters to shuffle

indicators.note: the smallest part of the word energy is its opening letter

explanation.surface: Pearl is distressed and listless after suffering a downturn in her health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns PEARLS into RELAPS, and 'minimal energy' adds E; 'having' joins them.
explanation.definitionFit: Falling ill again after seeming to recover is a recurrence, a return of a disease.

clue.text: A son among greatest or meanest?

indicators.note: the A and the son go among the letters of greatest

parts.note: the best is the greatest
S is the genealogical abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: Is one boy among the finest, or is he the stingiest of them all?
explanation.walkthrough: AS goes inside BEST after its B, giving B-AS-EST.
explanation.definitionFit: Base means low and contemptible, so the lowest or most ignoble is the meanest in character.

clue.text: What drinkers head for, creating an amount of pressure

definitions.meaning: a pub counter where drinks are served
a unit of atmospheric pressure used by meteorologists

explanation.surface: Drinkers making a beeline for the pub put pressure on the landlord.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creating' links the two definitions.
explanation.definitionFit: A pub's serving counter is what thirsty people make for, and a unit of air pressure is one hundred thousand pascals.

clue.text: Undesirable quality of 10 lasses getting drunk

indicators.note: lasses who are drunk are tipsy and jumbled, so the letters are mixed up

parts.note: the numeral 10 is written out as a word

explanation.surface: A gang of ten girls getting tipsy shows a regrettable lack of freshness.
explanation.walkthrough: The 10 is not a reference to clue 10; it is the number spelt out, shuffled with LASSES.
explanation.definitionFit: Being stale, like old bread or a tired joke, is lacking freshness, an unwelcome trait.

clue.text: Native gets married in prosperous region

indicators.note: the word for getting married sits inside the abbreviation for the region

parts.note: SE is the South East of England, traditionally its most prosperous region
to wed is to get married

explanation.surface: A local person ties the knot in a wealthy part of the country.
explanation.walkthrough: SE, the South East of England, is often seen as the country's richest region.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scandinavian born in Sweden is a native of that country.

clue.text: Container for money even now unopened

indicators.note: a word left unopened has lost its opening letter

parts.note: still means even now, as in 'he is still here'

explanation.surface: A cash box remains locked to this day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unopened' removes the first letter S from STILL.
explanation.definitionFit: A cash register or drawer in a shop holds the takings.

clue.text: Little dear out of sorts, not looked after properly

indicators.note: the phrase means jumbled or unsettled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A small darling is grumpy because nobody has cared for them well.
explanation.walkthrough: The ten letters of LITTLE DEAR are rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Being mistreated or abused means being handled badly instead of with proper care.

clue.text: Garment bringing sex appeal — not right being frontless!

indicators.note: losing its front means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: wrong means not right

explanation.surface: An item of clothing that adds allure, though wearing it backless is improper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'being frontless' drops the W from WRONG; 'bringing' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A Malaysian wraparound skirt of patterned cloth is an item of clothing.

clue.text: Little girl with French father, daughter mollycoddled

parts.note: Pam is a short form of the girl's name Pamela
pere is French for father
D is the genealogical abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A small girl, along with her French dad and daughter, was spoilt rotten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little' means a short form of a name, not a child.
explanation.definitionFit: To pamper or mollycoddle is to spoil someone with excessive indulgence and care.

clue.text: Mum, one with almost everything, is wanting million — nothing spiritual in that

parts.note: mater is old public-school slang for mother
the Roman numeral for one is I

indicators.note: almost means one letter short, so the last letter goes

parts.note: all means everything

explanation.surface: A mother who has nearly everything still craves a fortune, a woman with no soul.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wanting' links IS and M: the mother is wanting a million. 'almost' cuts ALL to AL.
explanation.definitionFit: A worldview valuing possessions and money above the soul leaves no room for the spiritual.

clue.text: Go round offering public entertainment with new ending — and opening

indicators.note: the final letter of the entertainment word is swapped for a different one

parts.note: a circus is a travelling public show
a vent is an opening or outlet

explanation.surface: A travelling show is offered, revised with a new finale and a new start.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue does not say what the new ending is: CIRCUS changes its last S to M, and the crossing letters confirm it.
explanation.definitionFit: To circumvent an obstacle is to find a way past it, to bypass or evade it.

clue.text: One vessel or another crossing a West Country river

indicators.note: the other vessel spans across the river by holding it inside

parts.note: a can is another kind of vessel, a container
the Tamar divides Devon from Cornwall

explanation.surface: A boat or another craft is ferrying across a river in south-west England.
explanation.walkthrough: The West Country is south-west England; the Tamar separates Devon and Cornwall. 'or' links the definition to the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A twin-hulled boat is a type of sailing vessel.

clue.text: See characters being strangled by someone's python

indicators.note: letters are squeezed inside the two words, held across their junction

explanation.surface: Watch someone's pet snake choking a victim.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of SOMEONE'S and the start of PYTHON.
explanation.definitionFit: To spot or catch sight of something is to notice it.

clue.text: See member of church try beers out after end of worship

indicators.note: the shuffled letters come after the letter from worship
the closing letter of worship is taken
out means wrong or disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A churchgoer is seen trying a few beers once the service ends.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' signals the anagram; the opening 'See' is only a link, though it tempts as part of the definition, as in a bishop's see.
explanation.definitionFit: An elder in a Presbyterian church is one of its office-holders.

clue.text: Coin with smell (not shilling)

indicators.note: not shilling means the shilling's letter is left out

parts.note: a scent is a smell
S was the abbreviation for the shilling, an old British coin worth one twentieth of a pound

explanation.surface: An old coin smells, though it is not a shilling.
explanation.walkthrough: The shilling was an old British coin, abbreviated s. Removing S from SCENT leaves the coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A hundredth of a dollar or euro is a small unit of currency.

clue.text: Contrary to expectation, needs locks for parts of building

parts.note: but introduces something contrary to what was expected
tresses are locks of hair

explanation.surface: Surprisingly, a lock is required on sections of the structure.
explanation.walkthrough: The plural TRESSES needs 'locks'; the scanned 'lock' lost its S. 'needs' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Supports projecting from a wall to strengthen it are structural features of a building.

clue.text: Squashed into row, gets even smaller

indicators.note: the contracted word goes into the row

parts.note: a tier is a row, as of seats

indicators.note: even squashed is the poetic contraction that drops its V

explanation.surface: A crowd crushed into a line becomes more cramped still.
explanation.walkthrough: E'en is the poetic contraction of even, so 'Squashed' drops its V; 'into' puts the result inside the row. 'gets' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Teeny means tiny, so the comparative means more tiny, more little.

clue.text: As something with the possibility of being made intimidating I'd ignored

definitions.text: As something with the possibility of being made

indicators.note: the letters for I'd are ignored, left out of the longer word

parts.note: formidable means intimidating
I'd without its apostrophe is spelt ID

explanation.surface: Something that might be made is being described, with a scary bit glossed over.
explanation.walkthrough: Take ID out of FORMIDABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: The suffix -able means capable of, so the word describes what can be shaped or created.

clue.text: Letter from abroad-nothing very big?

parts.note: O looks like zero, nothing
mega means very big

explanation.surface: A letter arrives from overseas: nothing huge, is it?
explanation.walkthrough: The 'letter from abroad' is a Greek letter, not a piece of post.
explanation.definitionFit: The last letter of the Greek alphabet is a foreign character.

clue.text: Organism needing oxygen — found in a beer that's off?

indicators.note: the oxygen symbol is found inside the jumbled beer letters
beer that is off has gone bad, so these letters are spoiled and rearranged

parts.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A microbe needing air is discovered in some beer that has gone sour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needing' links; O (oxygen) goes inside AEBER, the anagram of A BEER signalled by 'that's off'.
explanation.definitionFit: An aerobic microbe is a living thing that requires air to survive.

clue.text: Drive back partner initially in dance

indicators.note: the letter from partner goes in the dance

parts.note: a reel is a lively Scottish dance

indicators.note: initially means take the opening letter of partner

explanation.surface: During the dance, someone pushes their partner away.
explanation.walkthrough: A reel is a fast Scottish country dance; the partner's first letter goes inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To repel attackers is to repulse them, to force them away.

clue.text: Judicial order, one brought into residence breaking up

indicators.note: the house falling apart scrambles its letters

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: Someone moves into a home as it falls apart, and a court ruling follows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking up' rearranges RESIDENCE into DECREENIS; I is added at the end, and 'brought into' links. The surface hints at a marriage ending.
explanation.definitionFit: A provisional court ruling in a divorce precedes the final dissolution of the marriage.

clue.text: English bishop's sin

parts.note: RR is Right Reverend, the title of a bishop

explanation.surface: A church of England bishop has a sin to confess.
explanation.walkthrough: A bishop is styled the Right Reverend, abbreviated RR.
explanation.definitionFit: To sin is to go astray, to make a mistake morally.

clue.text: Holy teetotaller making a name in politics once

parts.note: pi is slang for pious, holy
TT stands for teetotal, someone who never drinks

explanation.surface: A pious non-drinker made his mark in politics long ago.
explanation.walkthrough: William Pitt the Elder and the Younger were 18th-century British prime ministers.
explanation.definitionFit: A father and son of that surname were famous British prime ministers in the eighteenth century.

clue.text: Style of a mansion getting mentioned

indicators.note: a word mentioned is spoken, so the word sounds the same when said

parts.note: a manor is a country mansion

explanation.surface: The design of a stately home is a topic of conversation.
explanation.walkthrough: MANOR said out loud matches the answer; 'of a' are links.
explanation.definitionFit: A way or mode of doing something is a style.

clue.text: Lambs err, unfortunately — see them traversing fields?

indicators.note: an unlucky mistake signals the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: Lambs wander off by mistake; watch the walkers crossing the meadows.
explanation.walkthrough: The anagram of LAMBS ERR gives walkers who cross the countryside; 'see' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Walkers who hike over the countryside cross pastures and open country.
